submission.note: Question-only contribution. Do not activate these questions in daily rotation until Phase B answer records have been committed and validated.

questions.prompt: Name a company that has developed or published a video game.
questions.context: The company may be a large publisher, an independent studio, a regional developer, or a historical company. It only needs one verifiable credit on a released video game.
questions.hint: Think about studios, publishers, regional specialists, and companies from the early arcade era onward.

include: A distinct, identifiable company or studio credited as the developer or publisher of at least one released electronic video game.
Companies from any country, platform, genre, or historical period.
Defunct companies and independently operated subsidiaries when the credited entity is separately identifiable.
Mobile, browser, arcade, console, computer, and handheld game developers or publishers.
exclude: Companies connected only as retailers, hardware manufacturers, distributors, licensors, or marketing partners without a development or publishing credit.
Individual games, franchises, people, esports teams, and informal groups that are not companies or identifiable studios.
Unreleased projects without a verifiable released-game credit.
acceptanceCriteria.canonicalization: Use the credited company or studio name as the canonical identity. Treat former names, spelling variants, punctuation variants, and language variants as aliases. Keep a parent company and a separately credited subsidiary distinct only when both are independently credited entities.

sourceGuidance.name: MobyGames company database
sourceGuidance.use: High-volume discovery index; verify each entry's actual developer or publisher role from game credits.

sourceGuidance.name: Official game credits and publisher catalogues
sourceGuidance.use: Primary verification for the company's development or publishing role.

questions.poolPotential: Very high; the discovery database indexes tens of thousands of company records, although only qualifying developer and publisher credits should be accepted.

questions.prompt: Name a feature film in which time travel is a major plot element.
questions.context: Films from any country, language, decade, or animation style qualify. Time travel must materially drive the story rather than appear only as a brief reference.
questions.hint: Consider films about time machines, temporal loops, people displaced into another era, and journeys into the future or past.

include: A feature-length live-action or animated film in which a central character travels to another point in time, or is repeatedly sent through a time loop that materially drives the plot.
Travel may be intentional or accidental and may move into the past or future.
Films from all national cinemas, including theatrical, television, and direct-to-video feature films.
exclude: Short films, individual television episodes, and series seasons.
Stories containing only flashbacks, flash-forwards, prophecies, memories, visions, or non-linear editing without an in-story temporal displacement.
Stories in which time travel is only mentioned or appears as an incidental background detail.
acceptanceCriteria.canonicalization: Use the film's original or best-established release title as the canonical name. Record translated titles, alternate release titles, transliterations, and punctuation variants as aliases; do not count a remake as the same film as its original.

sourceGuidance.name: AFI Catalog of Feature Films
sourceGuidance.use: Verify film identity, production details, and release format for eligible American films.

sourceGuidance.name: British Film Institute collections
sourceGuidance.use: Discover and verify films from international and historical cinema.

sourceGuidance.name: Official synopsis, credits, or distributor materials
sourceGuidance.use: Verify that temporal displacement is a material plot element; general genre labels alone are insufficient.

questions.poolPotential: High; include international cinema and animation rather than limiting research to well-known English-language releases.

questions.prompt: Name a brand whose logo depicts an animal.
questions.context: The animal must be visibly represented in an official brand logo or wordmark. The brand name alone does not qualify.
questions.hint: Look across food, sports, fashion, transportation, technology, entertainment, and regional businesses.

include: A distinct commercial, nonprofit, institutional, or product brand whose official logo visibly depicts an identifiable real or mythical animal.
Full-body animals, animal heads, silhouettes, heraldic animals, and clearly identifiable animal parts when they are part of the official logo.
Current or historical official logos, provided the brand identity and its logo can be verified.
exclude: Brands whose names merely contain an animal word when no animal is depicted in the logo.
Unofficial fan art, one-off advertisements, product mascots that are not part of the brand logo, and unrelated sponsor graphics.
Ambiguous abstract shapes for which an animal interpretation is speculative.
acceptanceCriteria.canonicalization: Use the brand's canonical public-facing name. Merge spelling, punctuation, and regional-name variants for the same brand; keep unrelated brands with similar animal imagery separate.

sourceGuidance.name: Official brand identity and press-kit materials
sourceGuidance.use: Primary proof that the animal artwork is an official logo.

sourceGuidance.name: Archived official websites and historical brand-guideline documents
sourceGuidance.use: Verify discontinued logos and legacy brands.

questions.poolPotential: High; search across industries and countries, and retain dated evidence for historical marks.

questions.prompt: Name an occupation whose workers commonly wear a recognizable uniform.
questions.context: The clothing must be a widely recognized, standardized part of performing the occupation in at least one substantial region or industry. It need not be identical worldwide.
questions.hint: Think about public service, transportation, healthcare, hospitality, trades, education, and ceremonial work.

include: A named occupation for which a recognizable uniform or standardized profession-specific work outfit is a common norm, formal requirement, or established occupational convention.
Occupations from any country, historical period, and employment sector.
Uniforms such as scrubs, service uniforms, flight uniforms, chef whites, academic or judicial robes, and other role-specific standard attire when the occupational connection is documented.
exclude: Jobs for which only ordinary everyday clothing or a generic business dress code is customary.
Occupations where only optional fashion, an individual employer's unusual dress choice, or generic personal protective equipment distinguishes the clothing.
A specific employer, rank, team, or uniform item offered instead of an occupation.
acceptanceCriteria.canonicalization: Use the standard occupation name as the canonical answer. Treat regional titles and synonymous job names as aliases, but do not merge genuinely different occupations merely because they share a uniform.

sourceGuidance.name: National occupational classifications and labour agencies
sourceGuidance.use: Establish the occupation's recognized name and scope.

sourceGuidance.name: Professional associations, licensing authorities, and employer uniform standards
sourceGuidance.use: Verify that the uniform is a common or formal occupational convention rather than an isolated dress choice.

questions.poolPotential: Medium to high; maximize international coverage and distinguish occupations carefully to avoid near-duplicate job titles.

questions.prompt: Name a character from the Naruto franchise.
questions.context: Characters from Naruto and its official sequel Boruto qualify, including major and minor named characters from the manga and officially released anime, films, or novels.
questions.hint: Look beyond Team 7 to the villages, clans, allied shinobi, historical figures, and sequel generation.

include: A named character who appears in an officially released Naruto or Boruto manga, anime, feature film, or licensed novel.
Major, supporting, minor, historical, deceased, and non-human characters, provided the character has an established name.
Official romanization variants and Japanese names when they refer to the same character.
exclude: Unnamed background characters, animals, techniques, locations, clans, and organizations.
Characters created solely for a video game, fan work, or unofficial crossover who do not appear in an official Naruto or Boruto publication or screen release.
Different aliases or titles for the same individual as separate answers.
acceptanceCriteria.canonicalization: Use the most commonly recognized character name as canonical. Store family-name/given-name order variants, official transliterations, former names, and titles as aliases when unambiguous.

sourceGuidance.name: NARUTO Official Site
sourceGuidance.use: Establish franchise scope and verify official Naruto/Boruto releases.

sourceGuidance.name: Shueisha / VIZ manga releases and official anime credits
sourceGuidance.use: Verify named characters and resolve transliteration or identity questions.

questions.poolPotential: High; include the full franchise and minor named characters, not just the principal cast.

questions.prompt: Name a character from the One Piece franchise.
questions.context: Any named character appearing in the official One Piece manga, anime, feature films, or licensed novels may qualify, including minor characters and characters from earlier arcs.
questions.hint: Think about pirates, marines, royalty, civilians, historical figures, and characters from every sea and island.

include: A named character who appears in an officially released One Piece manga chapter, anime episode, feature film, or licensed novel.
Major, supporting, minor, historical, deceased, and non-human characters with an established name.
Official romanization variants, epithets, and aliases when they identify the same individual.
exclude: Unnamed background characters, ships, crews or organizations as a whole, islands, species, powers, and objects.
Characters created only for a video game, fan work, or unofficial crossover who do not appear in an official One Piece publication or screen release.
Separate entries for aliases, titles, or alternate spellings of the same character.
acceptanceCriteria.canonicalization: Use the best-established character name as canonical. Preserve official romanization, name-order, epithet, and former-name variants as aliases when they refer to one individual.

sourceGuidance.name: ONE PIECE Official character search
sourceGuidance.use: Primary identity cross-check for listed characters; supplement it with manga and anime source material for exhaustive coverage.

sourceGuidance.name: Shueisha / VIZ manga releases and Toei Animation materials
sourceGuidance.use: Verify minor characters, appearances, and official spellings.

questions.poolPotential: Very high; the manga and anime contain a large international cast, so arc-by-arc research is appropriate.

questions.prompt: Name a national park anywhere in the world.
questions.context: Parks from every country and territory qualify, including parks whose official designation is expressed in another language. Include historical parks that were formally designated nationally.
questions.hint: Explore every continent and look beyond the best-known parks in North America and Africa.

include: A named protected area that has been formally designated as a national park by the relevant national-level government or statutory authority.
Current and former national parks, including official translated designations and recognized local-language names.
Marine national parks and national parks with unusual environments or cultural features.
exclude: State, provincial, municipal, or private parks without national-park designation.
Nature reserves, monuments, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, and World Heritage sites unless the same place also has an official national-park designation.
A region, mountain range, forest, or attraction that is not itself a designated national park.
acceptanceCriteria.canonicalization: Use the official park name in its local or best-established form. Keep separate parks distinct even when they share a translated name; store transliterations, translated names, and former official names as aliases.

sourceGuidance.name: Protected Planet / UNEP-WCMC and IUCN
sourceGuidance.use: Global discovery and cross-checking; filter specifically for national-park designations rather than accepting all protected areas.

sourceGuidance.name: National government park agencies and official gazettes
sourceGuidance.use: Primary confirmation of the national designation, official name, and historical status.

questions.poolPotential: Very high; use a country-by-country workflow and preserve the exact national designation for every accepted park.

questions.prompt: Name a genus of non-avian dinosaur.
questions.context: Use a formally named dinosaur genus. Include dinosaurs from every geological period and region, not only famous late-Cretaceous species.
questions.hint: Look across Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous discoveries, including small and fragmentary genera.

include: A formally published genus assigned to Dinosauria that is not an avian dinosaur.
Accepted valid genera from the Triassic, Jurassic, and Cretaceous, including herbivores, carnivores, and less familiar groups.
A genus supported by a recognized taxonomic database or a defensible published taxonomic treatment.
exclude: Pterosaurs, marine reptiles, other non-dinosaur reptiles, and living birds.
Informal nicknames, unpublished names, invalid names, and junior synonyms when they are not accepted as distinct genera.
Species epithets or individual fossil specimens submitted as though they were genus names.
acceptanceCriteria.canonicalization: Use the currently accepted genus spelling as canonical. Map historical spellings and documented synonyms to that accepted genus; do not count two names for the same taxon separately.

sourceGuidance.name: Paleobiology Database
sourceGuidance.use: Primary taxonomic and occurrence-data research source; inspect accepted-name and synonym relationships.

sourceGuidance.name: DinoPages PBDB-derived genus index
sourceGuidance.use: Convenient discovery index of non-avian dinosaur genera; trace accepted names back to Paleobiology Database records.

questions.poolPotential: High; a PBDB-derived index reports more than 1,600 valid non-avian dinosaur genera, subject to checking current taxonomic status.

questions.context: Butterfly species from every continent and habitat qualify, including skippers. Give a species-level name, not merely a family, genus, or subspecies.
questions.hint: Explore swallowtails, skippers, blues, brush-footed butterflies, moth-like groups, and tropical families.

include: A recognized species within the butterfly superfamily Papilionoidea, including skippers under modern classification.
Species from any geographic region, including island endemics, migratory species, and rare or recently described species.
Accepted scientific binomials and established common names that unambiguously identify one accepted species.
exclude: Moths outside Papilionoidea, other insects, and informal names that cannot be tied to a specific butterfly species.
Subspecies submitted as separate species unless a current taxonomic authority recognizes the taxon at species rank.
Synonyms, misspellings, and historical combinations counted separately from the accepted species.
acceptanceCriteria.canonicalization: Use the currently accepted scientific binomial as canonical. Map common names, former combinations, spelling variants, and recognized synonyms to the same species identity.

sourceGuidance.name: GBIF Backbone Taxonomy
sourceGuidance.use: Global discovery and accepted-name/synonym cross-checking at species rank.

sourceGuidance.name: Catalogue of Life / ChecklistBank
sourceGuidance.use: Compare accepted taxonomic names and synonymy; record checklist version and retrieval date.

sourceGuidance.name: Museum and specialist lepidopterist checklists
sourceGuidance.use: Resolve disputed species boundaries, regional names, and recent taxonomic changes.

questions.poolPotential: Very high; use global taxonomic checklists and deduplicate by accepted species identity rather than by common name.

questions.context: Any planet outside our Solar System that is listed as confirmed by the NASA Exoplanet Archive qualifies, including planets known mainly by catalog designation.
questions.hint: Look beyond the famous nearby systems to planets discovered by transit surveys, radial velocity, and microlensing.

include: A unique planet recorded as confirmed in the NASA Exoplanet Archive's current Planetary Systems (PS) data.
Planets in single-star, multi-star, circumbinary, and other confirmed planetary systems when the archive identifies a distinct planet.
Official proper names, host-star-plus-planet designations, and archive catalog designations as names for the same underlying planet.
exclude: Unconfirmed candidates, false positives, brown dwarfs not classified as planets, stars, and host systems submitted without a planet.
Duplicate archive solutions or alternate catalog labels for the same planet counted as separate answers.
Fictional planets and planets within our Solar System.
acceptanceCriteria.canonicalization: Assign one identity per confirmed planet. Prefer the established host-star-plus-letter designation as canonical when no IAU proper name is established; store proper names and catalogue aliases on that same record.

sourceGuidance.name: NASA Exoplanet Archive
sourceGuidance.use: Authoritative confirmation and current Planetary Systems (PS) table; exclude candidate-only tables.

sourceGuidance.name: NASA Exoplanet Archive API documentation
sourceGuidance.use: Retrieve the current Planetary Systems table and maintain a repeatable, dated research snapshot.

questions.poolPotential: Very high; the archive reported 6,470 confirmed planets on 2026-11-12, and its holdings are updated as literature is reviewed.
